newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Montenegrin PM snubs party, keeps ministers.
newsitem.headline: Montenegrin PM snubs party, keeps ministers.

text.p: Reformist Montenegrin Prime Minister Milo Djukanovic has survived attempts to force him from power and emerged on Friday with his Cabinet line-up intact.

After 11-hour-long talks, Montenegro's government issued a statement at midnight stressing a commitment to Yugoslavia and brushing aside charges by pro-Serbia hardliners that it was pursuing a separatist policy.
"...the government will focus its activities on ensuring economic and political stability and safety of its citizens," the press release said.

There was no mention of three senior officials whose resignation had been urged by Montenegrin President Momir Bulatovic and the governing board of the country's ruling Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS).

Deputy Prime Minister Slavko Drljevic, culture minister Goran Rakocevic and head of state security Vukasin Maras all appeared to have survived the hardliners' assault on Djukanovic and his pro-Western reformers.
In a conciliatory gesture, the government said it has accepted the resignation of its trade representative in Washington, Ratko Knezevic
Under pressure from Belgrade, the DPS Main Board voted through a no confidence motion in Djukanovic and demanded that he dump his most trusted cabinet allies.
The 35-year-old Djukanovic romptly resigned as vice-president of the party but political sources close to him had said he would rather quit as premier than desert his closest associates.
Djukanovic had strongly criticised Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic.

Djukanovic said in an interview last month that Yugoslavia had no future with a man like Milosevic at its helm, prompting Belgrade to accuse him of seeking Montenegro's seccession from what remains of Yugoslavia. Montenegro is Serbia's only partner in the federation.
Djukanovic has pursued an open door policy to the West in contrast to Belgrade, which is isolated by an outer wall of sanctions and faces Western pressure over human rights.

He enjoys widespread support and most opposition parties applaud his success in placing up to 95 percent of Montenegro's economy in private hands. Milosevic's Serbia has not even embarked on the privatisation road.
